neighbours.label: a lamenting interjection (Alas, Alack, oh!) inside a sentence of grief or regret
fire: The old king wept over his fallen son and said, Alas, my only heir is gone!
She read the letter twice and sighed, Alas, he will never come home again.
The poet stood by the grave and cried, Alack, how soon the young must die!
We hurried to the station but, alas, the last train had already left.
He searched the ruins all night and moaned, Alas, my books are ashes now.
The widow looked at the empty chair and whispered, Alas, the house is silent.
They waited for the ship for years, and oh! how bitter was the news at last.
The knight knelt by his horse and groaned, Alack the day I rode to war!
quiet: The old king smiled at his son and said, Look, my heir has come home!
She read the letter twice and said, Well, he will be home by Sunday.
The poet stood by the river and said, See how the swallows fly!
We hurried to the station and luckily the last train had not yet left.
He searched the attic all night and said, Here, my books are safe now.
The widow looked at the full table and said, Come, the soup is ready.
They waited for the ship for days, and the news came at last on Tuesday.
The knight knelt by his horse and said, Rest now, we ride at dawn.

predictions: 6/8 fire; neutral interjections and plain statements quiet
notes: Probe: 'cried, Alas' 0.783 on 'as', 'oh! how' 0.389, 'O Lord' 0.243, sentence-initial 'Alack' 0.138; 'Behold' 0.253 (peak on 'cried'), casual 'Oh, by the way' 0.052, 'Unfortunately' 0.036. Initial position is weak, so triggers are mid-sentence.
